work: Ibn ʿArabī, Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam. Covers chapter 12 only (the Word of Shuʿayb): chapter_12_shuayb.md, from chapter_12_shuayb_arabic.md.
about: Terminology record for the Fuṣūṣ translation, in the same shape as the Pardes Rimmonim lexicon at the root of this repository. Entries are keyed by Arabic. The first six entries record decisions made on 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-10; the rest record conventions the translation already had, taken from its own header and notes and marked as inherited. The chapter is not divided into numbered sections, so decisions cite a passage by a few of its words.

conventions.pronouns: Pronouns for God are lower-case throughout, including the quoted 'he' of huwiyya. (The Pardes translation capitalises them; the two projects differ by policy.)
conventions.brackets: Square brackets give Arabic terms at first occurrence, Qurʾān references, and words supplied for sense.

crossProject.note: The medieval Hebrew philosophical vocabulary was largely calqued from Arabic, so the two translations share terms. English is aligned where the sense is the same.

readerFields: Same meaning as in the Pardes lexicon: reader-facing text is entry.readerNote, entry.readerGloss and surfaceForms[form].readerGloss; everything else is the translator's working record.

ذات.etymology: Originally the feminine of ذو, 'possessor of': 'she who possesses', the bearer of the attributes. In ordinary Arabic بذاته means simply 'by itself', and in modern Arabic الذات is the word for 'the self'. The medieval Hebrew counterparts are עצם and עצמות.
ذات.notes: USER RULING (2026-11-09): ذات = 'self', not the customary 'essence'. The word names the thing's own self as against what it has or is related to. That is the contrast the chapter draws at its opening: the Real 'with respect to his self' is independent of the worlds, while lordship needs a world; 'and yet lordship ... is nothing other than this very self'. It also matches the ruling in the Pardes Rimmonim translation, where עצמות (the Hebrew counterpart) is 'Self' and the same question is asked of the Sefirot (Gate 4). The earlier translating session had resisted 'self'; the user reports finding the same rendering in Corbin, Alone with the Alone (passage not located here). 'Essence' is the usual choice in the English translations of the Fusus. RULES: (1) Lower-case 'self', in keeping with this translation's lower-case divine pronouns (the Pardes translation capitalises 'Self'; the two projects differ by policy). (2) التجلّي الذاتي = 'the autophany of the self'. (3) The logicians' adjective ذاتي, opposed to عرض, = 'intrinsic' ('intrinsic to it', 'an intrinsic definition'), matching the Pardes rendering of עצמי; this was done on the translator's initiative and flagged to the user as the most debatable of the changes, since 'essential definition' is the standard English for حدّ ذاتي. (4) 'Essence' is now free for ماهية. (5) Kept distinct from نفس = 'soul', which is the other Arabic word that can mean 'self'. SITES in ch. 12: 'with respect to his self [dhāt]'; 'the independence from the world that the self merits'; 'nothing other than this very self'; 'the autophany of the self [al-tajallī al-dhātī]'; ذاتي four times in the Ash'arite passage and once in its note.

ذات.readerNote: The self of a thing: what it is in itself, as against its attributes and its relations to other things. For the Real, the self is independent of the worlds, while the divine names each imply a relation to the world.

نفس.notes: USER RULING (2026-11-09): نفس = 'soul' wherever it stands as a noun. This frees 'self' for ذات and keeps the two apart in the sentence that needs both: 'his soul is not other than the one "he" refers to'. It also lines up with the Pardes translation, where the Hebrew split the same way: נפש kept the soul and עצמו took the reflexive. RULES: (1) The plain reflexive stays a reflexive: نفسه = 'himself', 'itself' ('God described himself [nafsahu] as having breath'; 'saying of himself'; 'in itself'; 'does not subsist by itself'). (2) The nafs / nafas pun (soul, breath) cannot be kept in English and is carried by note 5; 'soul' has its own old tie to breath (psyche, anima), so the link survives in idea. (3) The saying is 'whoever knows (recognizes) his soul knows (recognizes) his Lord'. (4) The passage on the philosophers and theologians, 'the soul and its essence', is the classical debate about the soul, which is one reason 'soul' suits better than 'self' there. COST accepted: the Delphic ring of 'from his self he recognized his self' is fainter as 'from his soul he recognized his soul'. SITES changed: 'from his own soul' (where the knower gives the Real the measure of each form); 'finds gloom within his soul' (the poem); 'From his soul he recognized his soul. And his soul is not other than ...'; 'Whoever recognizes his soul with this recognition has recognized his Lord'; 'the very one that person's "he" refers to'; 'the recognition of the soul and its reality'; 'the soul and its essence'. The last two of these changes ('within his soul', 'from his own soul') went beyond the user's explicit instruction and were flagged.

نفس.readerNote: The soul. The chapter's central claim is made about it: whoever recognizes his soul recognizes his Lord. The same Arabic word serves as the ordinary reflexive ("himself"), and it is close in sound to nafas, "breath".

ماهية.etymology: An abstract noun built from mā hiya, 'what is it?'. The Hebrew מהות is built the same way, from מה, and calques it.
ماهية.notes: RULING (2026-11-09, translator's proposal following the user's Pardes ruling, flagged to the user): ماهية = 'essence', not 'quiddity'. With ذات moved to 'self', 'essence' is free, and it matches מהות = 'essence' in the Pardes translation. One occurrence in ch. 12: 'in what they said about the soul and its essence [māhiyya]'.

decisions.rationale: Aligned with מהות = 'essence' in the Pardes translation.

ماهية.readerNote: The essence of a thing: what it is, the answer to the question "what is it?".

هوية.etymology: An abstract noun in -iyya from the pronoun huwa, 'he' or 'it'. Arabic has no verb 'to be' in simple sentences and huwa often does that work, which is why the early translators of philosophy used huwiyya for being and identity. God's self-designation by the pronoun is Qur'anic (112:1), and huwa alone is used as an invocation.
هوية.notes: USER RULING (2026-11-10): rendered by a phrase, not a noun: 'what "he" refers to', 'the one "he" refers to', 'who "he" is'. Reached after rejecting, in turn, 'being', 'identity', 'he-ness' and 'self'. THE SENSE: an abstract noun from the pronoun huwa. A pronoun, unlike a name, refers without describing. So the huwiyya is the Real as referred to with nothing said about him, in contrast to the Real as named by the divine names, each of which has its own content and implies a relation to the world. The chapter draws that contrast twice: 'with respect to his self' against what lordship demands, and 'as the one "he" refers to, and as related to the world through the realities of his most beautiful names'. Arabic grammar calls the third person 'the absent one' (al-ghā'ib), which ties the word to the unseen (ghayb). RELATION TO ذات: same referent, different sense, but not flatly identical. The text says the autophany of the self has the unseen as its reality, 'and it is what "he" refers to': the huwiyya is tied to hiddenness. Working gloss: the self as unseen. Whether later systematisers make it a distinct level is not settled here. WHY NOT THE ALTERNATIVES: 'being' (the former rendering) reads smoothly but will be heard as wujūd, loses the pronoun, and lets in a participatory reading that the Arabic excludes ('rather, it is the very huwiyya', with عين). 'Identity' pulls toward the relation of self-sameness (user's objection). 'He-ness' is exact but an opaque technical term (user: you might as well write Dasein). 'Self' reads well but merges the word with ذات. RULES: (1) The quoted pronoun is lower-case, 'he', like every other divine pronoun here; the same word is said of God and of a person, and the chapter's claim is that the two have one referent. (2) The pronoun itself is 'he', not 'He is': بقوله عن نفسه هو = 'when he says of himself, "he"'. (3) In the first passage 'it' is kept for the ambiguous antecedent (user: the pronoun refers back to the nearest noun, the unseen, and 'it' preserves the original). (4) In the Ash'arite passage the word has the philosophers' sense and is 'the thing itself'. (5) Do not soften the identity claim in the 'soul' passage: it is explicit in the Arabic, and Ibn 'Arabi puts the qualification in the forms and relations ('creation in one relation and Real in another, and the entity is one'), not in this noun. THE SIX OCCURRENCES: (i) 'it is what "he" refers to [huwiyya], which is his by right when he says of himself, "he." So "he" is his, always and forever.' (ii) 'as the one "he" refers to, and as related to the world ...' (iii) 'his soul is not other than the one "he" refers to, the Real; nor is anything in the cosmos ... other than the one "he" refers to — rather, it is that very one.' (iv) 'As for who "he" is: some servants are certain ...'; 'as to who "he" is ... as to who he is'. (v) 'he [the Lord] is the very one that person's "he" refers to, and his reality' (the possessive in the Arabic belongs to the person). (vi) 'the very thing defined, the thing itself'. A compact variant for (iii), 'not other than the Real's "he" ... it is that very "he"', was offered and not chosen. See note 10 of the translation.

هوية.readerNote: Literally "he-ness", from huwa, "he". It is the Real as referred to by the bare pronoun, with nothing said about him: hidden, unseen, prior to any name. The translation renders it by a phrase such as what "he" refers to.

هوية الحق.readerGloss: the one "he" refers to, the Real

وجد.partOfSpeech: noun (and the verbs of its root)
وجد.etymology: From w-j-d, 'to find'. The Hebrew translators of Arabic philosophy calqued it as מציאות, from מ-צ-א, also 'to find'.
وجد.notes: REVIEWED 2026-11-10, NO CHANGE: 'existence'. The user had felt 'existence' was not right in this chapter; on listing the passages it turned out that the noun occurs once and that the difficulty lay with huwiyya (then rendered 'being'). THE SEVEN USES OF THE ROOT in ch. 12: wujūdan = 'in existence' ('whether in existence or in supposition'); ījād = 'brought into existence'; mawjūdan = 'as existing'; mawjūdāt = 'existents'; yūjad = 'exists'; and the plain verb twice, yajidu / wajada = 'finds' ('finds gloom within his soul'; 'he finds God forgiving, compassionate'). THE ROOT SENSE is 'to find', and it is live for Ibn 'Arabi in a way it is not for the philosophers (cf. wajd, ecstasy). In this chapter the unveiling scene uses the plain verb: the dead man finds God other than his belief. An alternative for mawjūdan, 'as something there to be found', was noted and not adopted. CROSS-PROJECT: the Hebrew מציאות calques wujūd from a root that also means 'to find'. In the Pardes translation its technical count-noun use is 'manifestation'; that ruling does not carry over here, where the word has no such use.

candidates.contextNotes: With 'existents' for mawjūdāt, 'exists' for yūjad, 'brought into existence' for ījād.
Avoided, so that nothing is confused with the former rendering of huwiyya.

وجد.readerNote: Existence. The root also means "to find", and Ibn 'Arabi keeps that sense alive: what exists is what is found.

استحق.notes: OPEN (2026-11-10): the verb is rendered two ways in the chapter. 'The independence from the world that the self merits', and, in the huwiyya passage as the user approved it, 'which is his by right when he says of himself, "he"'. The mismatch was pointed out and not resolved. Unify when the chapter is next revised.
استحق.readerNote: To merit, to have by right.

حق.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'The Real', with 'God' for Allāh. Divine pronouns are lower-case throughout, by stated policy: the Arabic does not distinguish them and the chapter exploits the ambiguity. حقّ as an adjective is 'real'; حقّ وخلق = 'Real and creation'.
حق.readerNote: The Real: Ibn 'Arabi's usual name for God as what truly is.

تجلي.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Autophany' (self-showing); the verb is 'shows himself' or 'reveals himself'. Distinct from emanation (fayḍ): its concern is visibility. See note 8.
تجلي.readerNote: The Real's showing of himself. It never repeats, and each showing gives the heart its form.

عرف.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. The vocabulary of recognition: 'one who recognizes', 'recognition', 'recognize', so that recognizing and denying (ʿarafa / ankara) stay audible; معروف = 'the recognized'. علم is 'knowledge'. See notes 2 and 16.
عرف.readerNote: One who recognizes God, and the recognition itself, as distinct from knowledge (ʿilm).

عقد.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Belief' and 'conception', from a root meaning to tie a knot; عقدة = 'knot'. See notes 11 and 20.
عقد.readerNote: Belief, and what is believed. Each person sees the Real in the shape of what they have tied themselves to.

عين.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Entity'; also 'eye', a double sense the poem uses; and as an intensifier, 'the very'. See note 14.
عين.readerNote: An entity; also "eye". "No entity but the one entity" is also "no eye but the one eye".

قلب.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Heart'; تقلّب = 'shifting'; تقليب = 'being turned'. The root means to turn. See note 1.
قلب.readerNote: The heart, which by its name is the organ that turns: it takes the shape of each autophany.

رحم.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Compassion'; الرحمن is left as al-Raḥmān with '[the All-Compassionate]' at first occurrence. See notes 3 and 6.
رحم.readerNote: Compassion, which for Ibn 'Arabi is above all the giving of existence.

نفَس.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Breath'; تنفيس = 'relieving'; أنفاس = 'breaths' (instants). Puns with nafs. See note 5.
نفَس.readerNote: Breath. The world is breathed into existence, and renewed with every breath.

ألوهية.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Divinity' and 'lordship'; their correlates مألوه and مربوب are 'worshipper' and 'servant' (literally 'the god-ed' and 'the lorded-over'). عبد is also 'servant'. See the note on maʾlūh.
ألوهية.readerNote: Divinity and lordship: names that require a correlate, something to be god of and lord over, and so require a world.

عقل.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Intellect', related to the cord that hobbles a camel; قيد / تقييد = 'binding', إطلاق = 'release'. See note 15.
عقل.readerNote: The intellect, which binds: it fixes the matter to one description.

همة.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Concentrated intent'. See note 14.
همة.readerNote: Concern gathered to a single point.

خيال.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'The imaginal presence'. See note 17.
خيال.readerNote: The plane of imagination, where the absent becomes present.

استعداد.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Preparedness'.
استعداد.readerNote: The readiness of the heart to receive a given autophany, itself given by the autophany of the unseen.

غيب.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'The unseen' and 'the witnessed'; شهود = 'witnessing'; شهيد = 'a witness'.
غيب.readerNote: The unseen and the witnessed: the two domains, and the two autophanies.

جوهر.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Substance', 'accident', 'prime matter'. See note 27.
جوهر.readerNote: The theologians' terms: a substance bears accidents; prime matter underlies every form.

فناء.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Passing-away' and 'subsistence'.
فناء.readerNote: The passing-away of one creation at each autophany, and the subsistence of what the next one gives.

كشف.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Unveiling'; أهل الكشف = 'the people of unveiling'; الغطاء = 'the covering'.
كشف.readerNote: Direct disclosure, as against speculative thought.

فص.notes: ESTABLISHED before 2026-11-09 (earlier session). Recorded here from the translation's header and notes; not re-decided. 'Ringstone'; محلّ = its 'setting'. See note 9.
فص.readerNote: The stone set in a signet ring. Each chapter of the book is a ringstone.
